entries.title: The 3,500 kcal per pound rule is a rough guide that varies with body fat
entries.take: About 3,500 kcal (7,700 per kg) per pound of loss is only an average, and leaner people need less per unit lost.
entries.body: The rule says a cumulative deficit of 3,500 kcal equals one pound (32.2 MJ per kg) of weight loss. A model found it approximately matches obese people with more than 30 kg of body fat, and it overestimates the deficit needed for people with less body fat. Weight also responds slowly: the half time was about one year in a separate model. Use it to size a plan, then correct against the scale.
do: Use the rule to pick a starting deficit, then check the trend over three to four weeks.

entries.title: Aim to lose about 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week
entries.take: A pace of 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week is the usual advice for keeping muscle while getting leaner.
entries.body: A contest-prep review recommends 0.5 to 1 percent a week, and a later review prefers 0.5 percent or less for attenuating fat-free mass loss. In 24 athletes, both groups lost about 5.5 percent of body weight, but the 0.7 percent weekly group gained 2.1 percent lean mass and lost 31 percent of fat mass, while the group set 1.4 percent (1.0 percent achieved) kept lean mass unchanged and lost 21 percent of fat mass. McDonald's view is that faster loss mainly costs muscle when protein is low and lifting is light. At 80 kg (176 lb), 0.5 to 1 percent is 0.4 to 0.8 kg (0.9 to 1.8 lb).
do: Pick a weekly percentage, convert it to kg or lb, and check against your four-week trend.

entries.title: Deficits much beyond 500 kcal a day cost lean mass in lifters
entries.take: In a meta-regression, a deficit of about 500 kcal a day stopped lean-mass gains from training, while strength held up.
entries.body: A systematic review and meta-analysis of resistance training in an energy deficit found lean-mass gains were impaired against training without a deficit (effect size -0.57), but strength gains were comparable. The meta-regression put the point where gains were prevented at roughly 500 kcal a day. For people trying to preserve lean mass rather than add it, the authors advise avoiding deficits above that size. Short trials can differ: 40 young men on a 40 percent deficit with intense training gained 1.2 kg of lean mass on 2.4 g/kg of protein in 4 weeks.
do: Keep deficits at or below about 500 kcal a day if gaining or keeping muscle is the priority.

entries.title: Losing over 1 percent of body weight a week without high protein and heavy lifting
entries.take: Bigger deficits take a larger share of the loss from lean mass, and athletes who lost more slowly gained lean mass. Going faster needs high protein and heavy lifting.
entries.body: In 24 athletes lifting four times a week, a group set to lose 1.4 percent a week (1.0 percent achieved) kept lean mass unchanged and cut fat mass 21 percent, while a 0.7 percent loss gained 2.1 percent lean mass and cut fat mass 31 percent. A review found that lean tissue makes up a growing share of the loss as the deficit deepens, and a bigger share in leaner people. McDonald's view is that the old warnings about speed came from low-protein diets without lifting, and that lean dieters with high protein and heavy loads can go faster for short spells. Reviews recommend 0.5 to 1 percent a week.
do: Use 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week as the default pace.
If you go faster, keep protein high, keep lifting heavy and keep the fast spell short.

entries.title: Rate of loss
entries.take: Usual pace for keeping muscle; at 80 kg (176 lb) that is 0.4 to 0.8 kg a week.

entries.title: Deficit that stopped lean-mass gains
entries.take: In a meta-regression, deficits around this size prevented gains in lean mass in people doing resistance training.

entries.title: Energy per pound of weight lost
entries.take: The classic rule of thumb, which equals about 7,700 kcal per kg and varies with body fat.

entries.title: Energy deficit
entries.take: Eating less energy than you use. It is the one requirement for losing body fat. A daily deficit of 500 kcal is about 3,500 kcal a week.

entries.title: Deficit size versus expected weekly loss
entries.take: Approximate weekly loss for a daily deficit at 7,700 kcal per kg (3,500 per lb), for an 80 kg (176 lb) person. Leaner people tend to lose more weight than this.
rows: In range; near the limit seen for lean-mass trials
In range; hold protein and training high
Above 1%; faster than the athlete trial achieved

entries.title: Eat more protein when you diet: about 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of lean mass
entries.take: Lean lifters in a deficit kept more muscle with higher protein, around 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of fat-free mass.
entries.body: A review of six studies in lean, resistance-trained athletes in a deficit put protein needs at 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of fat-free mass, scaled up with the severity of the deficit and the leanness. The ISSN position gives 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of body weight. In a 4-week trial of 40 young men on a large deficit, 2.4 g/kg gained 1.2 kg of lean mass against 0.1 kg on 1.2 g/kg. A meta-analysis of 24 trials found higher protein held on to 0.43 kg more fat-free mass.
do: Set protein by your lean mass, and move up as the diet gets harder and you get leaner.

entries.title: Keep lifting while dieting, because training tells the body to keep muscle
entries.take: Resistance training reduced the lean mass lost in a diet, and strength was largely kept in deficit trials.
entries.body: An overview of 12 systematic reviews (149 studies) found resistance training limited lean mass loss during weight loss by about 0.8 kg. In six trials of older adults with obesity, training offset about 93 percent of the lean mass lost to calorie restriction. Strength gains in the deficit trials were comparable with and without a deficit.
do: Keep the main lifts heavy, and drop sets before you drop load.

entries.title: Short sleep shifts diet loss toward muscle and away from fat
entries.take: In ten adults, five and a half hours of sleep cut the fat share of weight lost by 55 percent.
entries.body: Ten overweight adults ate a reduced-calorie diet for 14 days in two conditions, with 8.5 or 5.5 hours in bed. Short sleep cut the fraction of weight lost as fat by 55 percent (1.4 vs 0.6 kg) and increased loss of fat-free mass by 60 percent (1.5 vs 2.4 kg). Hunger rose too. It is a very small and short crossover study, so treat it as a strong hint and not a finding.
do: Protect seven to nine hours in bed while dieting.

entries.title: Cutting protein and stopping lifting while dieting
entries.take: The two habits that protect muscle in a deficit are protein and heavy training, and dropping both costs lean mass.
entries.body: Higher protein held on to lean mass in trials of lean lifters, and training reduced lean loss by about 0.8 kg across an overview of reviews.
do: Keep protein high and lifts heavy until the diet ends.

entries.title: Protein in a deficit
entries.take: ISSN and review ranges for lean lifters dieting; raise it as the deficit and leanness grow.

entries.title: Protein and unprocessed food help control hunger, at least in the short run
entries.take: Protein reduced hunger in meal studies, and a ward trial found unprocessed meals led to about 500 kcal less intake.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 49 acute studies found protein lowered hunger and raised fullness, but long-term trials were inconclusive. In a ward study of 20 adults, ultra-processed meals led to 508 kcal a day more intake than unprocessed meals matched on presented calories, sugar, fibre and sodium, with weight up 0.9 kg against down 0.9 kg over two weeks. That is one small, short crossover trial.
do: Build meals around protein and whole foods before cutting portion size.

entries.title: Appetite rises as you lose weight, so hunger is part of the process
entries.take: In one 52-week trial, appetite rose enough to add about 100 kcal a day per kg of weight lost.
entries.body: In 153 people losing weight without being aware of the deficit, a model found eating drifted above baseline by about 100 kcal a day for each kilogram lost, more than three times the matching fall in energy expenditure. This is one analysis of one drug trial. It points to appetite, not metabolism, as the main pressure against keeping weight off.
do: Plan for hunger to rise late in a diet, and use protein, fibre and a fixed end date.

entries.title: Appetite rise per kg of weight lost
entries.take: In one trial, eating drifted above baseline by about this much for each kilogram lost.

entries.title: Water-rich fruit and vegetables lower hunger for the same calories
entries.take: In one year-long trial, women who ate more water-rich foods lost more weight and reported less hunger.
entries.body: In 97 women with obesity told to cut fat, one group was also told to eat more water-rich foods, mainly fruit and vegetables, with no calorie goal. Among completers after a year, that group lost 7.9 kg against 6.4 kg, ate a greater weight of food at a lower energy density, and reported less hunger. It is one trial in women with obesity, not lifters.
do: Fill half the plate with vegetables or fruit before adding the rest.

entries.title: Metabolic slowdown with dieting is real but smaller than most people fear
entries.take: Adaptation is real but small, tens to low hundreds of kcal a day in most studies, so check your log first.
entries.body: A systematic review of 33 studies (2,528 participants) found adaptive thermogenesis in 27, with lower or non-significant values in the better-designed studies. In 171 women, the drop after loss was 54 kcal a day, and in a subset of 46 it was no longer significant at one and two years. In 32 men on a 50 percent deficit for three weeks, true adaptation was 72 kcal a day. After 6 years, 14 Biggest Loser contestants were 499 kcal a day below prediction, an extreme case.
do: Check the log and weekends before blaming metabolism.

entries.title: Day-to-day weight changes are mostly water, so read the trend
entries.take: Two-week changes of 1 to 3 kg were largely fat-free mass and water, not fat, in free-living adults.
entries.body: In 46 adults, a unit of two-week weight change was 84 percent fat-free mass, and the energy density of 1 to 3 kg changes was about 2,380 kcal per kg, well below that of fat. Glycogen is stored with three to four parts water. Weight runs higher on Sunday and Monday in 80 adults, and fluid retention peaks at the start of menstrual flow in 62 women. None of these is fat gain.
do: Weigh at the same time under the same conditions, and judge the weekly average.
If you menstruate, compare the same week of one cycle with the same week of the next.

entries.title: A two-week stall is not proof your diet stopped working
entries.take: Check logging and weekend intake before cutting calories, since stalls are usually noise or under-logging.
entries.body: Ten people who reported not losing weight on under 1,200 kcal actually under-reported intake by 47 percent and over-reported activity by 51 percent. In a one-year trial of 48 adults, calorie-restricted participants stopped losing weight on weekends. Add water noise from the table above and a two-week stall tells you little. A real stall holds over three to four weeks of honest logging.
do: Wait three to four weeks, then cut by about 100 to 200 kcal or add steps.

entries.title: Cutting calories after a short stall
entries.take: Short stalls are mostly water and weekend noise, and cutting on them stacks deficit on top of a working plan.
entries.body: A two-week plateau can come from water, a missed weekend or logging drift, as 48 adults who stopped losing on weekends showed. Cutting calories on a stall moves you toward the 500 kcal limit sooner. McDonald's view is that cutting harder can also add stress-related water retention, which hides fat loss for longer. Wait three to four weeks, check the log, and only then change calories or steps.
do: Check the four-week trend and the log before changing calories.

entries.title: Energy per kg for short-term changes
entries.take: Two-week changes of 1 to 3 kg were mostly fat-free mass and water, so they carry less energy than fat.

entries.title: Adaptive thermogenesis (metabolic adaptation)
entries.take: A fall in energy use beyond what the loss of body mass explains, seen during and after weight loss. Studies find it ranges from small to modest.

entries.title: What moves scale weight day to day
entries.take: Short-term causes of scale changes that are not fat gain or loss.
rows: Each gram of glycogen is stored with three to four parts water
Weight is higher on Sunday and Monday, then falls
Fluid retention scores peak on the first day of flow
1-3 kg over two weeks is about 84% fat-free mass and water
Slow; reviews advise about 0.5-1% of body weight a week

entries.title: Weighing yourself regularly goes with more loss inside a programme
entries.take: Programmes that included self-weighing beat minimal care by 3.4 kg, and daily weighing did no better than weekly.
entries.body: A meta-analysis found 15 trials of multi-component programmes that included self-weighing lost 3.4 kg more than minimal or no intervention, with no significant difference between daily and weekly weighing. Only one study tested self-weighing alone, and it found no evidence of an effect. In two studies of female first-year students, daily weighing with feedback on the trend of the last 7 days kept weight steady while controls gained 3.1 and 2.0 kg. McDonald favours daily weigh-ins read as a running average. The scale is feedback inside a plan.
do: Weigh daily or on a fixed schedule, and act on the 7-day average, not on single days.

entries.title: Set point and settling point
entries.take: Two models of body weight: a defended set point, or a settling point where weight drifts with food and activity. A review finds both incomplete. McDonald's view is that the body resists loss far more than gain.

entries.title: Diet breaks and refeeds give mixed fat-loss results and may ease hunger
entries.take: Planned weeks at maintenance did not improve fat loss in lifters, and they lowered hunger.
entries.body: In 61 resistance-trained adults over 12 weeks, alternating three weeks of restriction with one week at maintenance gave the same fat and lean mass as continuous dieting, with lower hunger. A meta-analysis of 12 trials (881 participants) found the same body composition and a smaller drop in resting rate. A small 7-week trial found a weekly two-day carb refeed kept more lean mass (-0.4 vs -1.3 kg). Results in men with obesity favoured breaks.
do: Try a one- to two-week break at maintenance if hunger or training quality is slipping.

entries.title: The best diet is the one you can keep to, since types differ little
entries.take: Low-carb and low-fat diets lost about the same weight, so pick the one you can keep.
entries.body: A network meta-analysis of 48 randomized trials (7,286 people) found weight loss with any low-carbohydrate or low-fat diet, with small differences among named diets. A larger analysis of 121 trials (21,942 patients) found about 4.6 kg at 6 months with low carb and 4.4 kg with low fat. In a 12-month trial of 609 adults, the difference was 0.7 kg, not significant. Behavioural support added about 3.2 kg at six months in one analysis.
do: Choose the pattern that fits your food preferences and schedule.

entries.title: Intermittent fasting works by eating less, with no clear extra effect
entries.take: Time-restricted eating did not beat plain calorie control in long trials, though one pooled analysis disagrees.
entries.body: In 139 adults over 12 months, eating 8 am to 4 pm with calorie restriction lost 8.0 kg against 6.3 kg for calorie restriction alone, not a significant difference. A 12-week trial of 116 people found no advantage, and a 41-person feeding trial matched calories and found no effect on weight. A pooled analysis of 30 studies did report 1.46 kg more loss in matched comparisons. With lifting, an analysis of eight studies (221 participants) kept fat-free mass.
do: Use a fasting window only if it makes eating less easier for you.

entries.title: Meal frequency and late eating matter little for fat loss at equal calories
entries.take: Differences between meal patterns are small at equal calories; fewer meals showed about 1 kg more loss in one analysis.
entries.body: A network meta-analysis of 22 trials (647 people) found two meals a day slightly lowered weight against three meals or six, by about 1 kg, under equal calories. In 16 obese adults on the same deficit, three meals and three snacks did no better than three meals. A meta-analysis of 9 trials found earlier eating gave 1.2 kg more loss, and a controlled crossover trial found late eating raised hunger. Pick the pattern you can follow.
do: Choose a meal pattern around your day, and keep protein in each meal.

entries.title: Diet break and refeed
entries.take: A diet break is a planned stretch, often one to two weeks, at maintenance calories. A refeed is shorter, usually one or two days of higher carbohydrate.

entries.title: Time-restricted eating
entries.take: Eating all meals within a set daily window, such as eight hours, and fasting for the rest. It is one form of intermittent fasting.

entries.title: Weight lost tracked sticking to the diet, not which diet it was
entries.take: In one year-long trial, weight lost followed how closely people kept to their diet, with no link to the diet they chose.
entries.body: In 160 overweight or obese adults with heart-risk factors, assigned to Atkins, Zone, Weight Watchers or Ornish, mean one-year loss was 2.1 to 3.3 kg and only 50 to 65 percent finished. Loss correlated with self-reported adherence (r = 0.60) but not with diet type (r = 0.07). Adherence was self-reported and chosen by the participants, so this shows who did well, not that pushing adherence causes loss.
do: Pick the eating pattern you can see yourself keeping for a year.

entries.title: Exercise adds to fat loss, and daily movement drops on diets if you let it
entries.take: Exercise adds 1.5 to 3.5 kg of loss in reviews, and people on diets may move less outside the gym.
entries.body: An overview of 12 meta-analyses found exercise led to 1.5 to 3.5 kg of weight loss and similar results from aerobic and interval training when energy expenditure matched. The ACSM suggests 150 minutes a week as a floor and 200 to 300 for long-term loss. A systematic review of 36 articles found lower non-exercise activity in 63 percent of diet-only arms. In 16 overfed adults, NEAT explained the large differences in fat gain.
do: Set a daily step or activity floor and keep it during the diet.

entries.title: NEAT (non-exercise activity)
entries.take: Non-exercise activity thermogenesis: energy spent on walking, standing, fidgeting and chores. It can fall during a diet without you noticing.

entries.title: Getting very lean costs hormones, mood and training quality, so go carefully
entries.take: Long spells under about 25 kcal per kg of lean mass led to muscle loss and hormone and mood problems in men. In women, 30 marks rising risk, not a cut-off.
entries.body: Reviews of lean athletes link a long period at low energy availability to muscle loss, hormone disruption and psychological problems. In one natural bodybuilder, body fat fell from 14.8 to 4.5 percent and testosterone from 9.22 to 2.27 ng/mL, recovering after the contest. In 27 women dieting for a fitness show, sex hormones fell and most recovered within three to four months. The 30 figure comes from a five-day lab study; in 35 women over three cycles, risk rose steadily with no cut-off, and the 2025 Triad update moves away from a threshold. See the women area. Involve a coach and clinician.
do: Treat contest-level leanness as a short, supervised project, not a lifestyle.
See a clinician if periods stop or mood drops.

entries.title: Weight regain is common, and maintenance is possible with sustained habits
entries.take: Most people regain some weight. A minority keep most of it off, and they report steady activity and regular weighing.
entries.body: In 171 women, 52 percent of the weight lost was regained at one year and 89 percent at two. A meta-analysis of 29 US studies found the average person kept off more than 3 kg at five years. Among 2,886 National Weight Control Registry members, mean loss was 31.3 kg at entry and 23.1 kg at ten years; they report about an hour of activity a day and regular weighing. That link to activity is observational and self-selected: an overview of controlled trials found no significant effect of exercise training on maintenance. McDonald's rule is to return to maintenance promptly, not to climb in small steps for months.
do: After the diet, bring calories back to maintenance within about two weeks, then hold there.
Keep weighing, activity and protein up.

entries.title: Dieting with no end date and no plan for after
entries.take: Regain follows the diet for most people, and a plan for the exit matters as much as the deficit.
entries.body: In 171 women, 52 percent of lost weight was regained after one year and 89 percent after two. Registry members who kept it off kept activity, regular weighing and steady eating. Set an end date for the diet. McDonald's rule for the exit is to reach maintenance calories at once or within about two weeks, then hold there; no study here tests a slower climb.
do: Plan the exit: a target date, a maintenance range and a weekly weigh-in.
Return to maintenance calories at once or within about two weeks.

entries.title: A small surplus adds muscle, and a large surplus mostly adds fat
entries.take: A surplus of about 10 to 20 percent over maintenance is a common starting range for lifters, and nobody has proven the best size.
entries.body: A narrative review for physique athletes suggests 10 to 20 percent above maintenance, with advanced lifters more conservative. In 17 lifters over 8 weeks, a 15 percent surplus mainly increased fat gain rather than strength or muscle thickness. Another review finds the ideal surplus is unknown. If maintenance is 2,500 kcal, 10 to 20 percent is 250 to 500 kcal. Evidence is thin and short.
do: Start near the low end of the surplus and adjust to the scale.

entries.title: Recomposition works best for beginners, returners and people carrying more fat
entries.take: Gaining muscle while losing fat is realistic with high protein and hard training, and likely harder for lean, advanced lifters.
entries.body: In 40 young men on a roughly 40 percent deficit with heavy training and 2.4 g/kg of protein, lean mass rose 1.2 kg while fat mass fell 4.8 kg over four weeks. A review of six studies found that the groups that held on to or gained lean mass were among those with the highest body fat, the smallest deficit or a new training stimulus. Advanced lifters with low body fat have less room.
do: Use a small deficit or maintenance with high protein and progressive training.

entries.title: Treating a gaining phase as a licence to eat anything
entries.take: A large surplus mainly added fat in a trial, and extra fat has to be dieted off later.
entries.body: In 17 lifters, a 15 percent surplus mostly increased fat gain rather than strength or muscle thickness. A review suggests 10 to 20 percent for physique athletes, less for advanced lifters. The extra fat then has to be dieted off.
do: Use a measured surplus and watch the rate of weight gain.

entries.title: Surplus for a gaining phase
entries.take: Suggested range for novice and intermediate lifters in a physique-sport review; advanced lifters go lower.

entries.title: Rate of gain, novice to intermediate
entries.take: At 80 kg (176 lb) that is 0.2 to 0.4 kg (0.4 to 0.9 lb) a week.

entries.title: Recomposition
entries.take: Gaining muscle and losing fat over the same period. Body weight may hold steady or fall while the body changes shape.

entries.title: Rate of gain by training age
entries.take: Suggested pace of weight gain in a gaining phase; the research is thin and the rates are conservative.
rows: Mostly extra fat in an 8-week trial

entries.title: Size the deficit as a share of maintenance, not a fixed calorie number
entries.take: A percentage cut scales with the person: 20 percent is 360 kcal a day at 1,800 kcal maintenance and 600 kcal at 3,000.
entries.body: A fixed 500 kcal cut is more than a quarter of a small woman's intake and a sixth of a big man's. McDonald sets deficits as a share of maintenance and calls 10 to 15 percent small, 20 to 25 percent moderate and anything beyond 25 percent large. The same percentage gives a larger person a bigger daily gap, so they lose faster on paper. In resistance-training trials, lean-mass gains stopped at a deficit of roughly 500 kcal a day, and a 25 percent cut at high maintenance can pass that point.
do: Estimate maintenance and take 20 to 25 percent off; if you lift, check the result against the 500 kcal point.

entries.title: The same percentage deficit at two maintenance levels
entries.take: Daily deficit and a first-pass weekly loss at 7,700 kcal per kg (3,500 per lb). On far larger deficits, supervised dieters lost about a quarter less than the rule predicts in about 65 days.
rows: 180 kcal a day; about 0.16 kg (0.36 lb) a week
300 kcal a day; about 0.27 kg (0.6 lb) a week
Easy to keep; small enough for logging error to erase
A common middle ground for most dieters
Passes the 500 kcal guide for the larger person

entries.title: Running a 10 percent deficit while logging food loosely
entries.take: A deficit of 200 to 300 kcal a day is within reach of label and logging error, so it can vanish without you noticing.
entries.body: US rules let a label run up to 20 percent over the declared calories. Restaurant calories were accurate on average, but 19 percent of 269 items held at least 100 kcal more per portion than stated. In a review of 59 studies against doubly labelled water, most studies found people under-reported intake (see the label tolerance and under-reporting entries). On 2,000 kcal a day, a 10 percent error cancels a 10 percent deficit. McDonald's view is that small deficits suit lean, experienced dieters who weigh their food; for others a larger cut leaves room for error.
do: Weigh food and log everything if you choose a small deficit.
If your logging is rough, use a 20 to 25 percent cut instead.

entries.title: Losing weight quickly did not mean regaining it faster in a long trial
entries.take: Of 200 adults with obesity, those who reached the target had regained about 71 percent by week 144, whether the loss was rapid or gradual.
entries.body: A 12-week rapid and a 36-week gradual programme, both run through a hospital, aimed for 15 percent loss. Of the rapid group 81 percent reached 12.5 percent, against 50 percent of the gradual group; only they were followed, and completers had regained 70.5 and 71.2 percent by week 144. One person in the rapid group needed gallbladder surgery. In 262 obese, middle-aged women in a lifestyle programme, the fastest losers in month one had lost most at 18 months, an association only. McDonald argued in 2009 that fast loss can last if it builds habits; the trial came later and found no regain penalty, not an advantage.
do: Only consider a rapid diet inside a supervised programme with a clinician; it carries risks such as gallstones.
Lean lifters should still use the slower pace in the rate-of-loss entry.

entries.title: A fixed calorie cut slows to a plateau because the gap closes as you shrink
entries.take: On a fixed cut a shrinking body burns less, so loss slows and stops. Supervised dieters fell about a quarter short of the 3,500 rule in about 65 days.
entries.body: Each kg lost early holds less energy than fat, because water and lean tissue go too (see the week-four energy number). Even so, 103 adults with supervised or measured intake, on deficits near 1,440 kcal a day, lost 20.1 lb (9.1 kg) in about 65 days, against 27.6 lb (12.5 kg) predicted by the rule. For an average overweight adult, a validated model puts each lasting change of 100 kJ (24 kcal) a day at about 1 kg of eventual weight, half within a year. Eating less also trims the energy spent digesting food. To keep the pace, reopen the gap with less food or more movement.
do: Use a dynamic planner, such as the NIH Body Weight Planner, for forecasts beyond a few weeks.

entries.title: Eventual weight change per lasting change in daily intake
entries.unit: kJ a day per kg of change
entries.take: About 10 kcal a day per lb. A rule of thumb from one validated model: in an average overweight adult, half arrives within a year and 95 percent within about three.

entries.title: Reading a big first-week drop on low carb as fast fat loss
entries.take: An early drop on low carb is mostly stored glycogen and the water held with it, and fat loss did not speed up on a ketogenic diet in a ward study.
entries.body: Glycogen is stored with three to four parts water, so emptying it moves the scale while releasing little stored energy. In 17 overweight or obese men on a metabolic ward, swapping a high-carbohydrate diet for a ketogenic one with the same calories raised chamber energy expenditure slightly, by about 57 kcal a day, yet body fat loss slowed and fat-free mass loss rose. McDonald says the water returns once carbohydrate does. Judge any diet on the trend from week three or four onward.
do: Leave out the first two to three weeks when you compare diets or judge your rate of loss.

entries.title: Set up a fat-loss diet in order: calories, protein, fat, then carbohydrate
entries.take: Fix the calorie target first, then protein, then a moderate fat intake, and let carbohydrate fill whatever is left.
entries.body: A review for natural bodybuilders in contest prep sets calories for a loss of 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week, protein at 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of lean mass, fat at 15 to 30 percent of calories and carbohydrate as the remainder. McDonald uses the same order, holds that fatter dieters need less protein per kg, and starts fat at 20 to 25 percent of calories because very low-fat diets are hard to stick to. Example: 75 kg (165 lb) on 2,200 kcal, with 165 g protein (660 kcal) and 61 g fat (550 kcal), leaves about 248 g of carbohydrate. When calories must drop, carbohydrate usually gives way first.
do: Write down the four numbers before you choose foods.

entries.title: Athletes in a deficit should keep food around hard sessions and cut elsewhere
entries.take: When an athlete trims carbohydrate to diet, the cut should come from meals away from hard training, not from the meals that fuel it.
entries.body: A review of weight management in athletes lists eating around exercise among its core strategies, next to avoiding severe restriction and choosing foods of low energy density. It warns that severe restriction during hard training lowers strength, glycogen stores, concentration and the response to training. McDonald's view is that skipping food before or after hard sessions to save calories only hurts training, because the deficit sets fat loss either way. Easy, low-intensity sessions are the exception.
do: Keep some carbohydrate and protein before and after hard sessions, and take cuts from other meals.

entries.title: Athletes should diet in a low-intensity training block, not close to competition
entries.take: Plan fat loss for the off-season or a general preparation block, and aim for a weight you can hold for most of the year.
entries.body: A review on athletes' weight advises finding a healthy weight that can be kept for most of the year, so little has to come off before competition, and allowing enough time to get there safely. McDonald places fat loss in the general preparation phase, when volume is high and intensity lower, using only a small calorie cut. In his view most sports have an ideal leanness, and going below it costs muscle and performance. The IOC statement on REDs links low energy availability to health and performance harm.
do: Map the season and pick the diet weeks first.
Choose a target weight you can hold without constant dieting.
If periods, mood or performance change while dieting, see a sports doctor or dietitian.

entries.title: Energy in each kg lost at week four of a diet
entries.take: Rose to about 6,000 by week six in 23 overweight adults. Still below the rule's 7,700, so each kg lost early needs a smaller deficit than the rule assumes.

entries.title: Rigid and flexible restraint
entries.take: Two styles of holding back on food. Rigid control runs on fixed rules and forbidden foods, all or nothing. Flexible control allows any food in limited amounts and evens out over days.

entries.title: Flexible control of eating goes with lower weight and fewer binges than rigid rules
entries.take: In large surveys, people who allowed limited amounts of any food weighed less and binged less than people who ran on strict food rules.
entries.body: Among 54,517 people in a weight-loss programme and a population sample of 1,838 aged 14 and over, rigid control was linked with higher BMI and more frequent, more severe binges. Flexible control was linked with lower BMI, fewer binges and a better chance of losing weight over a year. In 188 non-obese women, rigid dieting went with eating disorder symptoms and low mood, and flexible dieting did not. These are associations, not trials, so they show who does well rather than proving the cause.
do: Plan some favourite foods into the week instead of banning them.
If food rules or binges feel out of your control, see a doctor or an eating disorder specialist.

entries.title: Treating one off-plan snack as a ruined diet
entries.take: A 200 kcal treat is under a tenth of a 3,500 kcal weekly deficit. Giving up on the day because of it is what costs you.
entries.body: All-or-nothing rules make a small lapse feel like failure. McDonald describes a common response: the day feels lost, so the person eats freely until it ends. Rigid control was linked with more frequent and more severe binges in a large survey. McDonald's view is that the snack itself does little harm, especially if the next meals are a little smaller, and that calling planned meals off the diet 'cheats' keeps the good-or-bad framing that drives the spiral. He uses planned free meals and diet breaks instead.
do: After an unplanned treat, carry on with the next meal, or trim it slightly.
Call planned off-plan meals free meals, and plan them in advance.

entries.title: Dropping whole fruit from a fat-loss diet
entries.take: In a six-week trial in adults with obesity, a calorie-restricted diet with fruit lost more weight than one that kept fructose very low.
entries.body: In 131 adults, mostly women, on restricted diets of 1,500 to 2,000 kcal, a group eating under 20 g of fructose a day lost 2.83 kg, while a group getting 50 to 70 g from natural fruit lost 4.19 kg. It was one short trial, and the authors still advised less added fructose. In a year-long trial in 97 women with obesity, eating more water-rich foods such as fruit went with less hunger (see the energy density entry). McDonald's view is that whole fruit helps many dieters feel fuller, and he advises it over juice.
do: Keep a few portions of whole fruit in the day and count them in your calories.
Choose whole fruit over juice.

entries.title: When the trend says change, move calories about 10 percent and wait again
entries.take: Adjust intake or activity in steps of about a tenth, then reassess after two to three weeks, or four if water swings hide the trend.
entries.body: Lifts falling with sound training, or loss well beyond the plan, means ease off: McDonald adds about 10 percent to calories or drops some cardio, as falling strength can signal muscle loss. Loss short of the plan after about three weeks of honest logging means cut intake or add activity by about a tenth, then look again in two to three weeks. A rate on target needs nothing. Take a break at maintenance if intake is already low or sleep, mood or training are slipping (see the very-lean entry). His wider rule: replace a change that shows nothing in about four weeks and keep one that works.
do: Write down the weekly loss you expect before you start.
Change one thing at a time.

entries.title: Holiday weight gain is small on average, but it tends to stay
entries.take: In 195 adults, weight rose about 0.4 kg over the winter holidays, far below the 2.3 kg (5 lb) often claimed, and the gain was not lost in the months after.
entries.body: Adults were weighed from late September to early March and again the following autumn. The mean gain from mid-November to January was 0.37 kg, with no significant change before or after, and the season's net 0.48 kg had not reversed by the next autumn in the 165 who returned. The spread was wide, about 1.5 kg either way. McDonald's view is that the jump after one large meal is mostly carbohydrate, salt and water, not fat. His advice is to plan a few treats, start parties with protein and vegetables, and not write off the season after one rich meal.
do: Weigh yourself a week after a holiday meal, not the next morning.
Choose the treats you most want rather than grazing on all of them.

entries.title: Skipping breakfast did not hurt weight control in short trials
entries.take: In a meta-analysis of short trials, people assigned to breakfast ate about 260 kcal a day more and weighed slightly more than people assigned to skip it.
entries.body: In randomised trials in adults, breakfast eaters weighed 0.44 kg more (7 trials) and took in about 260 kcal a day more (10 trials), though trials were short and mostly of low quality. The energy spent digesting food depends on how much you eat, not how often. McDonald's view is that smaller women on low intakes often do better with three or four filling meals than with six tiny ones. Skipping breakfast differs from eating late, which the meal timing entry covers.
do: Eat breakfast if it keeps you full to lunch, and skip it if it does not.

entries.title: Cutting out dairy for a diet or contest prep
entries.take: Dairy did not change weight overall in a meta-analysis, but in calorie-restricted trials it gave slightly more weight and fat loss.
entries.body: Across 29 randomised trials (2,101 people), dairy had no overall effect on weight. In short or energy-restricted trials it lowered weight, and pooled over 22 trials body fat fell a modest 0.45 kg, with the benefit confined to short or restricted trials. In long-term trials or ones without a calorie limit it went with slightly more weight, so count it. McDonald's guess is that dropping it before shows dates from bulking on whole milk; he found no mechanism, and adds that dairy is a main source of calcium. With a milk allergy or lactose intolerance, follow your clinician's advice.
do: Count dairy in your calories and protein like any other food.

entries.title: Setting protein as a percentage of calories during a diet
entries.take: A fixed share of calories gives less protein as calories fall, just when lean lifters in a deficit likely need more. Set protein in grams per kg instead.
entries.body: At 25 percent of calories, protein is 175 g on 2,800 kcal but 125 g on 2,000 kcal, a drop of 50 g. A review of six studies in lean, resistance-trained athletes in a deficit concluded the need likely rises with the size of the deficit and with leanness, and set it per kg of fat-free mass. McDonald makes the same point for every nutrient: needs follow body size, so a percentage means little until you know the calories behind it. Fix protein in grams first and share out the rest.
do: Fix protein in grams first, for example 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of lean mass for a lean lifter in a deficit.

entries.title: Glycaemic index (GI)
entries.take: How far a food's carbohydrate raises blood glucose against the same amount from glucose or white bread. Fat, protein and fibre in a meal lower it, and in studies GI did not change how much fat people burned.

entries.title: Targeted and cyclical ketogenic diets
entries.take: Ketogenic diets adapted for hard training. A targeted version adds a small dose of carbohydrate around sessions; a cyclical one alternates several low-carbohydrate days with one or two days of high carbohydrate.

entries.title: Planned time off the diet did not cut total weight loss in a trial
entries.take: In 142 adults in a behavioural weight-loss programme, scheduled breaks from dieting left total loss at 5 and 11 months unchanged.
entries.body: Researchers told one group to stop all weight-loss efforts for six weeks midway, and another for two weeks three times, hoping to provoke relapse. Logging, dieting and self-weighing lapsed in the breaks (exercise did not), loss slowed or reversed slightly, and people resumed quickly. Overall loss matched the control group. McDonald's view is that a break the dieter chooses keeps a sense of control, so a holiday that would derail the diet anyway is better planned as one. See the diet break entry for trials at maintenance.
do: If a holiday or busy spell will stop your diet, McDonald's practice is to plan it as a break with an end date.

entries.title: McDonald keeps carbohydrate at 120 to 150 g a day or more on a diet break
entries.take: McDonald sets a carbohydrate floor of about 120 to 150 g a day for a diet break, on the view that thyroid hormone needs it.
entries.body: In obese patients on low-calorie diets of 360 to 1,200 kcal, blood T3, the active thyroid hormone, fell only when carbohydrate was 120 g a day or less, whatever the calories, and reverse T3 stayed raised at 40 to 50 g. It is one 1982 study of hormone levels during dieting, not of fat loss, and it did not test a break at maintenance. McDonald's view is that a break kept very low carb misses part of its point. Fat-loss results from breaks in trials are mixed (see the diet break entry).
do: On a break, McDonald's practice is at least 120 to 150 g of carbohydrate a day.

entries.title: McDonald spaces diet breaks by body fat, so leaner dieters take them sooner
entries.take: In McDonald's practice, lean dieters take a break every 4 to 6 weeks, while people carrying more fat go 12 to 16 weeks between breaks.
entries.body: His reasoning is that the hormonal and metabolic response to dieting grows as people get leaner (see the bodycomp entry on lean tissue loss speeding up), so the leanest need relief most often. He sets the break near estimated maintenance, often 5 to 10 percent under it, for 10 to 14 days, and wants contest dieters to start early enough to fit one in. No trial has compared spacing by body fat, and fat-loss results from breaks in trials are mixed (see the diet break entry).
do: McDonald's advice: put the break in the timeline before the diet starts, so a deadline cannot squeeze it out.

entries.title: Higher protein after a diet halved weight regain in one trial
entries.take: In 148 overweight to moderately obese adults after a diet, about 48 g a day of extra protein halved regain over 3 months, all of it fat-free mass.
entries.body: Participants first lost weight on a 4-week very low-energy diet of about 500 kcal a day, an intake for medical supervision only, then were randomised for 3 months of maintenance. The extra-protein group ate 18 percent of energy as protein against 15 percent, regained half as much weight, consisting only of fat-free mass, and felt fuller while energy intake did not differ. McDonald keeps protein at the dieting level after a diet ends, mainly because post-diet hunger is high. This was one trial in overweight to moderately obese adults; lean lifters were not studied.
do: McDonald's practice: keep protein at your dieting level for the first weeks of maintenance.

entries.title: After a physique contest, regain came first as water and later mostly as fat
entries.take: In 15 natural physique athletes, weight and body water rose soon after competing, and fat mass climbed about 2 kg by 4 to 6 weeks later.
entries.body: Seven men and eight women were measured within a week before a show, within a week after and 4 to 6 weeks later. Weight rose 2 kg between the first two visits, body water rose about 1.9 L in 8 of them, and lean mass by ultrasound rose and then held. By the last visit fat mass had gone from 7.7 to 10.0 kg. Resting metabolic rate, 92 percent of predicted before the show, was back near normal. It was a pilot study. McDonald's view is that the post-diet 'rebound' only regains lost muscle and glycogen, not new size.
do: McDonald's practice: return to maintenance calories before any surplus; see the diet exit entries.
If eating feels out of control after a show, get help from a sports dietitian or clinician.

entries.title: McDonald puts the low days of an intermittent restriction plan on rest days
entries.take: Two very low days a week lost as much as a daily cut in overweight women. McDonald's view is that the low days must miss hard training.
entries.body: In 107 premenopausal women with overweight or obesity, about 2,710 kJ (650 kcal) on 2 days a week lost 6.4 kg over 6 months against 5.6 kg on a daily 25 percent cut, a difference that was not significant. McDonald's view is that this kind of plan, or alternate-day fasting with low days near a quarter of maintenance, only suits a lifter whose low days can fall on rest days. The trial did not test placement or include lifters. Days near 650 kcal are a large cut; with a medical condition or medication, check with a clinician first.
do: McDonald's practice: set low days on rest days, or choose a daily cut if your training days are fixed.

entries.title: Gut bacteria went with a difference of about 150 kcal in energy absorbed
entries.take: In 21 inpatients, shifts in gut bacteria went with changes in the calories lost in stool, about 150 kcal in lean people.
entries.body: Twelve lean and nine obese adults ate diets of 2,400 and 3,400 kcal on a ward while stool energy was measured. Changing the amount of food changed the gut bacteria quickly, and in lean participants a 20 percent rise in one bacterial group went with about 150 kcal more energy harvested. This is an association in a small group. McDonald's view is that such differences alter how much energy you absorb without breaking energy balance; he wrote in 2009 that no one knew how to change it usefully.

entries.title: Nutrient balance (protein, carbohydrate and fat balance)
entries.take: Intake minus oxidation for one nutrient. In 54 adults in a chamber, the body matched carbohydrate and protein burning to intake, so day-to-day surpluses and gaps landed almost entirely on fat balance.

entries.title: Alcohol cut the fat burned by about a third on the day it was drunk
entries.take: In 8 men in a chamber, alcohol at a quarter of daily energy cut fat burning by about a third that day, while carbohydrate and protein burning held.
entries.body: The men drank about 96 g of alcohol a day, either on top of their usual food or in place of some fat and carbohydrate. Both ways, 24-hour fat oxidation fell by 31 to 36 percent, during the hours alcohol was being cleared, and energy expenditure rose 4 to 7 percent. The authors concluded that drinking beyond energy needs probably favours fat storage. McDonald's view is that the body keeps no store of alcohol, so it is always burned off first. This was a heavy intake in a small group.
do: Count drinks in your daily intake; see the alcohol entries in the nutrition area.

entries.title: The higher protein in low-carb diets, not the low carb, drove loss in one trial
entries.take: In 132 adults with obesity, high-protein diets lost more over a year than normal-protein ones, while low-carb against normal-carb made no difference.
entries.body: Four diets crossed protein (about 1.1 against 0.7 g per kg) with carbohydrate (low or normal), on a third of energy needs for 3 months, a very low intake, then two thirds for 9 months. At 12 months the high-protein groups had lost 12.8 kg against 8.9 kg, low-carb groups did no better than normal-carb ones, and changes were unrelated to fat content. McDonald's view is that low-carb diets work mainly through the protein they bring, and that more protein is the single most useful diet change. Intakes that low belong under medical supervision.
do: Set protein first, then choose carbohydrate and fat to suit your food preferences.

entries.title: What any fat-loss diet needs before its details matter
entries.take: Check a plan against these before worrying about meal timing or macro ratios. The first group is essential; the second decides whether you can keep it up.

groups.name: Essential
items: Enough protein for your body fat and training
Fruit and vegetables for vitamins and minerals

groups.name: Makes it last
items: A plan for lapses and breaks
Habits you can carry into maintenance

entries.title: The same surplus added 4 to 13 kg in different men, and twins responded alike
entries.take: Twelve pairs of young identical twin men overfed by 1,000 kcal a day gained 4.3 to 13.3 kg, with brothers far more alike than unrelated men.
entries.body: The men were overfed on 84 days within a 100-day period, about 84,000 kcal in total. Mean gain was 8.1 kg. Variation between pairs was about three times that within pairs, and the authors pointed to genes governing whether energy is stored as fat or lean tissue and how resting expenditure responds. McDonald's view is that such differences change how fast weight moves, not whether energy balance applies; no one gains on a real deficit. See the NEAT number in the body composition area for one route.
do: Judge your own response by your scale trend, not by someone else's results on the same plan.

entries.title: Eating more of a food because it is labelled low-fat or diet-approved
entries.take: Women told a yogurt was low-fat ate more at the next meal than after a yogurt of similar calories labelled high-fat.
entries.body: In 48 healthy, non-dieting women, the label changed lunch intake, and total intake that day was still higher after the 'low-fat' yogurt. Women given no label showed the opposite pattern. McDonald's view is that every popular diet soon gets its own approved snacks and bars, often as calorie-dense as what they replace, and that people eat more of them because they feel allowed, until loss stalls.
do: Log diet-approved foods by their calories, not their label.

entries.title: Setting a goal of losing a third of your body weight in one go
entries.take: Sixty women with obesity aimed to lose 32 percent of their weight. After 48 weeks and a 16 kg loss, nearly half had not reached even the result they called disappointing.
entries.body: Before treatment the women named a goal, a dream, a happy, an acceptable and a disappointed weight. They rated a 17 kg loss disappointing and 25 kg acceptable, far beyond the modest losses guidelines recommend. McDonald's view is that goals set too large or too fast make a good result feel like failure, and people quit when progress slows. Expect the rate to fall as you go (see the fixed calorie cut entry).
do: Count a lasting loss of about 10 percent as success, the clinical yardstick McDonald cites.
McDonald's practice: break a large loss into stages with maintenance between them.

entries.title: False hope syndrome
entries.take: Polivy and Herman's name for a cycle of repeated self-change attempts driven by unrealistic hopes about how fast, how far and how easily change will come, and what it will bring. Failure is followed by a fresh attempt.

entries.title: Resting metabolic rate in formerly obese adults
entries.take: Formerly obese adults against never-obese controls of equal body composition, pooled in 1999. Later studies are mixed; see the metabolic adaptation entry.

entries.title: A ketogenic diet lost no more fat than a moderate-carb diet in a controlled trial
entries.take: In 20 sedentary adults with obesity on controlled food for 6 weeks, ketogenic and moderate-carb diets lost similar weight and fat.
entries.body: One diet began near 5 percent of energy as carbohydrate and 60 percent fat; the other was about 40 percent carbohydrate and 30 percent fat. Weight loss was 6.3 and 7.2 kg and fat loss 3.4 and 5.5 kg, neither difference significant. The ketogenic group did worse on an inflammation marker and on rated vigour. McDonald's view is that, with protein matched, ketosis gives no fat-loss edge, though some people control food intake better without starchy foods. See the first-week drop entry for a ward study.
do: Pick low or moderate carbohydrate by what you can stick to and train on, not for a fat-burning edge.

entries.title: Protein against carbohydrate: loss at 12 months in four diets
entries.take: Mean loss in 132 adults with obesity: 3 months at a third of energy needs (a supervised-only intake), then 9 at two thirds. Low carb did not beat normal carb (see the protein entry).

entries.title: Negative calorie illusion (dieter's paradox)
entries.take: The mistaken belief that adding a healthy food to an unhealthy meal lowers its calories. In Chernev's studies the error was larger in people most concerned with their weight.

entries.title: In a diet, McDonald cuts heavy volume from the start and keeps the load
entries.take: McDonald's practice is to drop heavy volume by up to two thirds when a diet begins, hold the usual loads, and fill any time saved with cardio or light work.
entries.body: His reasoning is that recovery falls in a deficit and a few quality heavy sets beat many poor ones. Support comes from maintenance studies outside a deficit (see the maintenance dose entry in recovery). In one trial of 70 adults, a third or even a ninth of the build-up dose kept muscle size for 32 weeks in those aged 20 to 35, but not in those aged 60 to 75. No trial cited here tested a calorie deficit, so older dieters may need more.
do: McDonald's practice: in a diet, keep 2 to 4 heavy sets per muscle group, as little as once a week, at your usual loads.

entries.title: Antidepressants differ in their effect on weight, so raise changes with the prescriber
entries.take: A meta-analysis of 116 studies linked some antidepressants to weight gain and others to little change or slight loss, with wide individual variation.
entries.body: Amitriptyline, mirtazapine and paroxetine went with a greater risk of gain. Fluoxetine and bupropion went with some loss, for fluoxetine only early in treatment. Others had little short-term effect, and effects tended to grow over the long term. Some comparisons rested on few studies. McDonald's view is that these drugs act mainly through appetite, sometimes activity, so ordinary diet and activity changes still apply. A weight change is a reason to talk to the prescriber, never to stop or switch a medicine on your own.
do: If your weight changes on a psychiatric medicine, raise it with your prescriber; do not stop or change it yourself.

entries.title: After surgery or injury, McDonald's advice is to heal first and diet later
entries.take: In McDonald's view, healing raises energy needs and a deficit may slow repair, so a little fat gained while recovering is the smaller problem.
entries.body: He advises eating at maintenance or slightly above while recovering, and dieting only after the injury has healed. Whether to lose fat before a planned operation is a decision for the surgical team, who may also set rules on eating, fasting and supplements beforehand. This entry rests on his judgment, not on a trial cited here.
do: Follow your surgical team's or physiotherapist's advice on eating before and after an operation.

hall-2007.title: What is the required energy deficit per unit weight loss?
hall-2007.support: The rule of thumb approximately matches the predicted energy density of lost weight in obese subjects with an initial body fat above 30 kg but overestimates the cumulative energy deficit required per unit weight loss for people with lower initial body fat.

hall-2011.title: Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight
hall-2011.support: The bodyweight response to a change of energy intake is slow, with half times of about 1 year; adults with greater adiposity have a larger expected weight loss for the same change of energy intake.

helms-2014-prep.title: Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation
helms-2014-prep.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
helms-2014-prep.support: Caloric intake should be set at a level that results in bodyweight losses of approximately 0.5 to 1%/wk to maximize muscle retention; 2.3-3.1 g/kg of lean body mass of protein.

garthe-2011.title: Effect of Two Different Weight-Loss Rates on Body Composition and Strength and Power-Related Performance in Elite Athletes
garthe-2011.journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
garthe-2011.support: 24 athletes; 0.7% vs 1.4% weekly loss; LBM increased 2.1% in the slow group and was unchanged (-0.2%) in the fast group.

roberts-2020.title: Nutritional Recommendations for Physique Athletes
roberts-2020.support: Slower rates of weight loss (<=0.5% of body mass per week) are preferable for attenuating the loss of fat-free mass, with diet breaks and refeeds possibly beneficial.

murphy-2021.title: Energy deficiency impairs resistance training gains in lean mass but not strength: A meta‐analysis and meta‐regression
murphy-2021.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
murphy-2021.support: Meta-regression: an energy deficit of ~500 kcal/day prevented gains in lean mass; strength gains were comparable between conditions.

helms-2014-protein.title: A Systematic Review of Dietary Protein During Caloric Restriction in Resistance Trained Lean Athletes: A Case for Higher Intakes
helms-2014-protein.journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
helms-2014-protein.support: Six studies; protein needs for energy-restricted resistance-trained athletes are likely 2.3-3.1 g/kg of FFM scaled upwards with severity of caloric restriction and leanness.

jager-2017.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise
jager-2017.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
jager-2017.support: Higher protein intakes (2.3-3.1 g/kg/d) may be needed to maximize the retention of lean body mass in resistance-trained subjects during hypocaloric periods.

longland-2016.title: Higher compared with lower dietary protein during an energy deficit combined with intense exercise promotes greater lean mass gain and fat mass loss: a randomized trial
longland-2016.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
longland-2016.support: 40 young men, 4 weeks at about 40% energy deficit with resistance and interval training; 2.4 vs 1.2 g/kg protein: lean mass +1.2 vs +0.1 kg, fat mass -4.8 vs -3.5 kg.

wycherley-2012.title: Effects of energy-restricted high-protein, low-fat compared with standard-protein, low-fat diets: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
wycherley-2012.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
wycherley-2012.support: 24 trials with 1063 individuals; high-protein diets mitigated reductions in fat-free mass (0.43 kg) and resting energy expenditure.

sardeli-2018.title: Resistance Training Prevents Muscle Loss Induced by Caloric Restriction in Obese Elderly Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sardeli-2018.support: Six RCTs in obese elderly individuals; resistance training reduced 93.5% of calorie-restriction-induced lean body mass loss.

bellicha-2021.title: Effect of exercise training on weight loss, body composition changes, and weight maintenance in adults with overweight or obesity: An overview of 12 systematic reviews and 149 studies
bellicha-2021.support: Overview of 12 systematic reviews (149 studies); exercise led to weight loss of 1.5-3.5 kg; resistance training reduced lean mass loss during weight loss; no difference between aerobic and HIIT when energy expenditure is equal.

nedeltcheva-2010.title: Insufficient Sleep Undermines Dietary Efforts to Reduce Adiposity
nedeltcheva-2010.support: 10 overweight adults, 14 days of caloric restriction with 8.5 or 5.5 h of sleep opportunity; sleep curtailment decreased the proportion of weight lost as fat by 55% and increased loss of fat-free mass by 60%.

hall-2019.title: Ultra-Processed Diets Cause Excess Calorie Intake and Weight Gain: An Inpatient Randomized Controlled Trial of Ad Libitum Food Intake
hall-2019.support: 20 weight-stable adults in a ward; energy intake was greater on the ultra-processed diet by 508 kcal/day; +0.9 kg vs -0.9 kg over 2 weeks.

kohanmoo-2020.title: Effect of short- and long-term protein consumption on appetite and appetite-regulating gastrointestinal hormones, a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
kohanmoo-2020.support: 49 acute and 19 long-term publications; acute protein ingestion suppresses appetite; results of long-term trials are inconclusive.

polidori-2016.title: How Strongly Does Appetite Counter Weight Loss? Quantification of the Feedback Control of Human Energy Intake
polidori-2016.support: 153 patients in a 52-week trial; weight loss led to a proportional increase in appetite, eating above baseline by about 100 kcal/day per kilogram of lost weight.

peos-2021.title: Continuous versus Intermittent Dieting for Fat Loss and Fat-Free Mass Retention in Resistance-trained Adults: The ICECAP Trial
peos-2021.support: 61 resistance-trained adults over 12 weeks; no difference in fat mass or fat-free mass between intermittent and continuous restriction; the intermittent group had lower hunger.

campbell-2020.title: Intermittent Energy Restriction Attenuates the Loss of Fat Free Mass in Resistance Trained Individuals. A Randomized Controlled Trial
campbell-2020.journal: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology
campbell-2020.support: 27 resistance-trained adults over 7 weeks; the two-day carbohydrate refeed group kept fat-free mass (-0.4 kg vs -1.3 kg) and resting metabolic rate better than the continuous group.

byrne-2018.title: Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study
byrne-2018.support: 51 men with obesity; intermittent restriction gave greater weight loss (14.1 vs 9.1 kg) and fat loss than continuous restriction over the same 16 weeks of restriction.

poon-2024.title: Effects of intermittent dieting with break periods on body composition and metabolic adaptation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
poon-2024.support: 12 randomized trials with 881 participants; no group differences in body mass or fat loss; resting metabolic rate fell less after intermittent dieting with breaks.

nunes-cl-2021.title: Does adaptive thermogenesis occur after weight loss in adults? A systematic review
nunes-cl-2021.support: 33 studies with 2528 participants; adaptive thermogenesis observed in 27; well-designed studies reported lower or non-significant values.

martins-2020.title: Metabolic adaptation is not a major barrier to weight-loss maintenance
martins-2020.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
martins-2020.support: 171 overweight women followed 2 years; metabolic adaptation -54 kcal/d after loss and not significant at 1 or 2 years; participants regained 52% and 89% of weight lost at 1 and 2 years.

muller-2015.title: Metabolic adaptation to caloric restriction and subsequent refeeding: the Minnesota Starvation Experiment revisited
muller-2015.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
muller-2015.support: 32 nonobese men; 3 weeks at -50% of energy needs; adaptive thermogenesis 108 kcal/d, of which 72 kcal/d was true adaptive thermogenesis.

fothergill-2016.title: Persistent metabolic adaptation 6 years after “The Biggest Loser” competition
fothergill-2016.support: 14 Biggest Loser participants; at 6 years RMR was 704 kcal/day below baseline and metabolic adaptation was -499 kcal/day.

bhutani-2017.title: Composition of two-week change in body weight under unrestricted free-living conditions
bhutani-2017.support: 46 adults; two-week free-living weight changes were largely fat-free mass and water: 84% of a unit change in weight was fat-free mass; energy density of 1-3 kg changes averaged 2380 kcal/kg.

orsama-2014.title: Weight Rhythms: Weight Increases during Weekends and Decreases during Weekdays
orsama-2014.support: 80 adults, 4,657 measurements; higher weight early in the week (Sunday and Monday), decreasing during the week.

kreitzman-1992.title: Glycogen storage: illusions of easy weight loss, excessive weight regain, and distortions in estimates of body composition
kreitzman-1992.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
kreitzman-1992.support: Glycogen is stored in hydrated form (three to four parts water); changes in total body potassium in 11 subjects after 4 days on a very-low-calorie diet reflected glycogen mobilization.

white-2011.title: Fluid Retention over the Menstrual Cycle: 1-Year Data from the Prospective Ovulation Cohort
white-2011.support: 765 menstrual cycles in 62 healthy women; fluid retention scores peaked on the first day of menstrual flow and were lowest in the mid-follicular period.

lichtman-1992.title: Discrepancy between Self-Reported and Actual Caloric Intake and Exercise in Obese Subjects
lichtman-1992.support: Subjects reporting diet resistance under-reported actual food intake by 47 percent and over-reported physical activity by 51 percent.

authors: Washington University School of Medicine CALERIE Team
racette-2008.title: Influence of Weekend Lifestyle Patterns on Body Weight
racette-2008.support: 48 adults; on weekends calorie-restricted participants stopped losing weight.

johnston-2014.title: Comparison of Weight Loss Among Named Diet Programs in Overweight and Obese Adults
johnston-2014.support: 59 articles reporting 48 randomized trials (7286 individuals); significant weight loss with any low-carbohydrate or low-fat diet; differences between named diets were small.

ge-2020.title: Comparison of dietary macronutrient patterns of 14 popular named dietary programmes for weight and cardiovascular risk factor reduction in adults: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials
ge-2020.support: 121 eligible trials with 21,942 patients; low carbohydrate and low fat diets had a similar effect at six months on weight loss (4.63 vs 4.37 kg).

gardner-2018.title: Effect of Low-Fat vs Low-Carbohydrate Diet on 12-Month Weight Loss in Overweight Adults and the Association With Genotype Pattern or Insulin Secretion
gardner-2018.support: 609 adults; weight change at 12 months was -5.3 kg for low-fat vs -6.0 kg for low-carbohydrate (difference 0.7 kg, 95% CI -0.2 to 1.6).

liu-2022.title: Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss
liu-2022.support: 139 patients with obesity; 12 months; weight loss -8.0 kg with time-restricted eating plus calorie restriction vs -6.3 kg with calorie restriction alone (not significantly different).

lowe-2020.title: Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters in Women and Men With Overweight and Obesity
lowe-2020.support: 116 participants, 12 weeks; time-restricted eating was not more effective for weight loss than eating throughout the day.

maruthur-2024.title: Effect of Isocaloric, Time-Restricted Eating on Body Weight in Adults With Obesity
maruthur-2024.support: 41 adults, isocaloric feeding for 12 weeks; weight decreased 2.3 kg with time-restricted eating and 2.6 kg with usual eating; any effect in earlier studies may be due to lower calorie intake.

fernandes-2025.title: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials Comparing Time-Restricted Eating With and Without Caloric Restriction for Weight Loss
fernandes-2025.support: 30 studies, 1341 participants; time-restricted eating reduced body weight even in isocaloric comparisons (-1.46 kg).

keenan-2020.title: The Effects of Intermittent Fasting Combined with Resistance Training on Lean Body Mass: A Systematic Review of Human Studies
keenan-2020.support: Eight studies; intermittent fasting paired with resistance training generally maintains LBM and can promote fat loss.

ashtary-2021.title: Effects of intermittent fasting combined with resistance training on body composition: a systematic review and meta‐analysis
ashtary-2021.support: Eight studies including 221 participants; intermittent fasting plus resistance training reduced fat mass by 1.36 kg relative to non-IF diets without a significant effect on fat-free mass.

schwingshackl-2020.title: Impact of Meal Frequency on Anthropometric Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
schwingshackl-2020.support: 22 RCTs with 647 participants; two meals a day probably slightly reduces body weight compared with three (-1.02 kg) or six meals (-1.29 kg) under isocaloric conditions.

cameron-2010.title: Increased meal frequency does not promote greater weight loss in subjects who were prescribed an 8-week equi-energetic energy-restricted diet
cameron-2010.support: 16 obese adults, 8 weeks at the same energy restriction; no differences in weight loss, appetite or gut peptides between 3 meals plus 3 snacks and 3 meals a day.

young-2022.title: Distribution of energy intake across the day and weight loss: A systematic review and meta‐analysis
young-2022.support: Nine RCTs; in an energy-reduced diet, earlier distribution of intake gave greater weight loss (-1.23 kg; 95% CI -2.40 to -0.06).

vujovic-2022.title: Late isocaloric eating increases hunger, decreases energy expenditure, and modifies metabolic pathways in adults with overweight and obesity
vujovic-2022.support: Randomized crossover trial; late eating increased hunger and decreased waketime energy expenditure with nutrient intake, activity, sleep and light controlled.

donnelly-2009.title: Appropriate Physical Activity Intervention Strategies for Weight Loss and Prevention of Weight Regain for Adults
donnelly-2009.support: A minimum of 150 min/wk of moderate-intensity physical activity for overweight adults; 200-300 min/wk recommended for long-term weight loss.

silva-2018.title: What is the effect of diet and/or exercise interventions on behavioural compensation in non-exercise physical activity and related energy expenditure of free-living adults? A systematic review
silva-2018.support: 36 articles, 1561 participants; compensation (lower NEAT or NEPA) observed in 26 of 70 arms, representing 63% of diet-only, 27% of combined and 23% of exercise-only arms.

levine-1999.title: Role of Nonexercise Activity Thermogenesis in Resistance to Fat Gain in Humans
levine-1999.support: 16 nonobese volunteers overfed by 1000 kcal/day for 8 weeks; changes in NEAT accounted for the 10-fold differences in fat storage.

fagerberg-2018.title: Negative Consequences of Low Energy Availability in Natural Male Bodybuilding: A Review
fagerberg-2018.journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
fagerberg-2018.support: A prolonged energy availability under 25 kcal/kg FFM results in muscle loss, hormonal imbalances and psychological problems; a more tempered approach (>25 kcal/kg FFM) might result in less muscle loss.

rossow-2013.title: Natural Bodybuilding Competition Preparation and Recovery: A 12-Month Case Study
rossow-2013.journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
rossow-2013.support: Case study of one natural bodybuilder; body fat fell from 14.8% to 4.5% and testosterone from 9.22 to 2.27 ng/mL during preparation, returning to baseline after competition.

hulmi-2017.title: The Effects of Intensive Weight Reduction on Body Composition and Serum Hormones in Female Fitness Competitors
hulmi-2017.support: 27 dieting women and 23 controls; ~12% body weight loss over 4 months; hormones including leptin, T3, testosterone and estradiol fell and menstrual irregularities increased; most recovered within 3-4 months.

loucks-2003.title: Luteinizing Hormone Pulsatility Is Disrupted at a Threshold of Energy Availability in Regularly Menstruating Women
loucks-2003.journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism
loucks-2003.support: 29 young women; luteinizing hormone pulsatility was unaffected at 30 kcal/kg LBM/day of energy availability, and disrupted below this threshold.

mountjoy-2023.title: 2023 International Olympic Committee’s (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)
mountjoy-2023.support: 2023 IOC consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport; health and performance outcomes of low energy availability in female and male athletes.

thomas-jg-2014.title: Weight-Loss Maintenance for 10 Years in the National Weight Control Registry
thomas-jg-2014.support: 2886 National Weight Control Registry participants; mean loss 31.3 kg at entry, 23.8 kg at 5 years and 23.1 kg at 10 years; more than 87% still maintaining at least a 10% loss at years 5 and 10.

wing-2005.title: Long-term weight loss maintenance
wing-2005.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
wing-2005.support: Members have lost an average of 33 kg and maintained the loss for more than 5 y, with about 1 h/d of physical activity, self-monitoring of weight and a consistent eating pattern across weekdays and weekends.

anderson-2001.title: Long-term weight-loss maintenance: a meta-analysis of US studies
anderson-2001.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
anderson-2001.support: 29 US studies; 5 years after structured weight-loss programs the average individual maintained a weight loss of >3 kg and a reduced weight of >3%.

rosenbaum-2010.title: Adaptive thermogenesis in humans
rosenbaum-2010.support: Over 80% of people return to pre-weight-loss body fatness after otherwise successful weight loss; adaptive thermogenesis is operant in lean and obese individuals.

iraki-2019.title: Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review
iraki-2019.support: A hyper-energetic diet (~10-20%) with a target weight gain of ~0.25-0.5% of body weight per week for novice/intermediate bodybuilders; advanced bodybuilders should be more conservative.

helms-2023.title: Effect of Small and Large Energy Surpluses on Strength, Muscle, and Skinfold Thickness in Resistance-Trained Individuals: A Parallel Groups Design
helms-2023.support: 21 trained lifters randomized, 17 completers over 8 weeks; maintenance vs 5% vs 15% energy surplus; faster rates of body mass gain primarily increase rates of fat gain rather than augmenting strength or muscle thickness.

slater-2019.title: Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training
slater-2019.support: The specific energy surplus required to facilitate muscle hypertrophy is unknown; there is clear evidence of an anabolic stimulus from an energy surplus.

helms-2019.title: Towards a Sustainable Nutrition Paradigm in Physique Sport: A Narrative Review
helms-2019.support: Physique athletes have higher body image and eating disorder rates; best-practice suggestions include dietary flexibility and slower weight loss.

hall-kahan-2018.title: Maintenance of Lost Weight and Long-Term Management of Obesity
hall-kahan-2018.support: Obesity interventions typically result in early weight loss followed by a weight plateau and progressive regain.

dansinger-2005.title: Comparison of the Atkins, Ornish, Weight Watchers, and Zone Diets for Weight Loss and Heart Disease Risk Reduction
dansinger-2005.support: 160 adults randomised to 4 popular diets; 1-year weight loss 2.1 to 3.3 kg, 50 to 65 percent completed; weight loss associated with adherence (r = 0.60) but not diet type (r = 0.07).

ello-martin-2007.title: Dietary energy density in the treatment of obesity: a year-long trial comparing 2 weight-loss diets
ello-martin-2007.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
ello-martin-2007.support: Obese women (n = 97) over 1 y; the group eating more water-rich foods lost 7.9 vs 6.4 kg, ate a greater weight of food at lower energy density and reported less hunger.

madigan-2015.title: Is self-weighing an effective tool for weight loss: a systematic literature review and meta-analysis
madigan-2015.journal: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity
madigan-2015.support: Fifteen trials of multi-component interventions including self-weighing vs no or minimal intervention: -3.4 kg; no significant difference between weekly and daily weighing; only one study of self-weighing as a single strategy and no evidence it was effective.

speakman-2011.title: Set points, settling points and some alternative models: theoretical options to understand how genes and environments combine to regulate body adiposity
speakman-2011.support: The set point model is consistent with many biological aspects of energy balance but does not explain the rise in body weight since the 1980s; the settling point model accommodates environmental characteristics but struggles with biological and genetic aspects.

levitsky-2006.title: Monitoring weight daily blocks the freshman weight gain: a model for combating the epidemic of obesity
levitsky-2006.support: Female freshmen weighed themselves each morning and received feedback from the most recent 7 days of weights. The untreated controls gained 3.1 kg and 2.0 kg, whereas weight gain of the experimental groups was 0.1 kg and -0.82 kg, values not significantly different than zero.

mcdonald-bmi-weighing.title: Of BMI and Weighing Frequency
mcdonald-bmi-weighing.support: Backs the advice to weigh often, act on a rolling average and pair the scale with a second measure.

forbes-2000.title: Body Fat Content Influences the Body Composition Response to Nutrition and Exercise
forbes-2000.journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
forbes-2000.support: In experiments of at least 3-weeks' duration, the weight gain of thin people comprises 60-70% lean tissues, whereas in the obese it is 30-40%. There is an inverse curvilinear relationship between initial body fat content and the proportion of weight loss consisting of lean tissue.

mcdonald-single-digit.title: Muscle Loss While Dieting to Single Digit Body Fat Levels
mcdonald-single-digit.support: Backs his explanation of why lean dieters lose more lean tissue and what protects it.

mcdonald-set-points.title: Set Point Settling Points and Bodyweight Regulation Part 1
mcdonald-set-points.support: Backs his reading that weight defence is lopsided and that set point and settling point both operate.

mcdonald-transition-phase.title: The Transition Phase Between Dieting and Gaining
mcdonald-transition-phase.support: His rule for ending a diet: reach estimated maintenance calories at once or within about two weeks and hold there, rather than a long stepwise climb. A judgment, not a trial result.

mcdonald-adjusting-diet.title: Adjusting the Diet
mcdonald-adjusting-diet.support: His view that water shifts mask weekly fat loss, more so with hard deficits and heavy activity, and his scheme: cut 10% if loss lags, add 10% or trim cardio if performance falls, recheck in 2 to 3 weeks. A judgment, not a trial.

lieberman-2018.title: Menstrual Disruption with Exercise Is Not Linked to an Energy Availability Threshold
lieberman-2018.support: Thirty-five sedentary, ovulatory women age 18 to 24 yr completed a diet and exercise intervention over three menstrual cycles. The likelihood of a MD decreased by 9% for each unit increase in EA (odds ratio, 0.91; 95% confidence interval, 0.84-0.98). No specific value of EA emerged as a threshold below which MD were induced.
